case_title: Ramesh and Others v. State of Haryana
accused_victim_relationship: Spouse (Ramesh is the husband); other accused are the husband's younger brother Suresh, Suresh's wife Saroj and the mother-in-law Prem; prior physical abuse and dowry-related harassment alleged
evidence_type: Dying declaration recorded by Judicial Magistrate; medical evidence (MLR, doctor's fitness endorsement, autopsy); recovery of kerosene container; oral evidence of brother (PW-4), father (PW-3, hostile)
confession: No confession relied on. Disclosure statement by Ramesh (Ex.PM) led to recovery of a kerosene container; the Court did not rely on it as a confession.
aggravating_circumstances: Prior assault (victim allegedly thrown into a well a year earlier) and repeated dowry-related beatings, as described in the dying declaration
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of all charges by the Sessions Court
high_court_outcome: Appeal against acquittal allowed; all four convicted. s.302/34 IPC: rigorous imprisonment for life and fine Rs.10,000 (1 year in default); s.498A/34 IPC: two years RI and fine Rs.2,000 (six months in default)
offence_finally_established: Murder (IPC s.302 read with s.34); cruelty by husband and relatives (IPC s.498A read with s.34)
neutral_facts: The victim, a married woman, was sleeping in the matrimonial house in the early hours of 20 September 1999 when the accused persons came to her room. According to the victim's statement, the husband and his younger brother had earlier beaten her. Two other family members held her arms, the husband sprinkled kerosene on her and the brother lit a matchstick, setting her ablaze. Neighbours extinguished the fire. The accused persons took the victim to a hospital, where she was found to have about 100% burns. The attending doctor certified that she was fit to make a statement. A judicial magistrate then recorded her statement in the presence of the medical officer, and the doctor again certified that she remained fit during the recording. The victim died within a few hours. A post-mortem found the burns to be ante mortem and sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course. Following a disclosure by the husband, police recovered an empty plastic kerosene container. The victim's father and brother, examined as witnesses, did not support the prosecution account. The brother said the husband had been with him at his house on the night of the incident and that they learned of the burns at about 4 a.m. Hospital records showed that the husband had brought the victim to hospital and had her admitted. The victim's statement also alleged years of dowry demands and repeated beatings by the in-laws.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from about 100% burn injuries; the post-mortem opinion was that the burns were ante mortem and sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 and s.498A, each with s.34); 2 finally upheld
motive: alleged: continued dowry demands (money, scooter, buffalo) by the husband and in-laws, as stated in the dying declaration
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration recorded by the Judicial Magistrate (PW-11) with the doctor's fitness certificates before and after recording; medical officer present during recording; hospital records showing the husband brought and admitted the victim; post-mortem evidence of ante mortem burns
witness_credibility: Magistrate PW-11 found credible; his cross-examination answer read out of context. PW-4 (brother) found to have been won over by the accused and his evidence discarded as false in view of hospital records. PW-3 (father) turned hostile; the Court attributed the hostility to a culture of compromise.
post_offence_conduct: The husband and other accused took the victim to PGIMS, Rohtak and got her admitted, per hospital records and the defence case
trial_duration: offence: 20 September 1999; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 30 May 2014; Supreme Court: 22 November 2016
legal_representation: Accused: Praveen Kr. Aggarwal, Upendra Pratap Singh, Sanjay Jain (Advocates). State: Jagdeep Kr. Sharma, Gyanendra Kr., Vishwa Pal Singh (Advocates).
investigation_status: FIR registered (No. 254, 28 September 1999); investigation completed; charge sheet under s.173(2) Cr.P.C. filed; case committed to Sessions Court
procedural_irregularity: Trial court gave no weight to the doctor's fitness certification, gave no reasons for disbelieving the Magistrate, and did not discuss whether precautions were taken in recording the dying declaration
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted. High Court: acquittal set aside and all four convicted (30 May 2014). Supreme Court: appeal dismissed, conviction upheld.
prosecution_argument: The incident occurred in the matrimonial house, the statement was recorded after the victim reached hospital, and the authorities were satisfied she was fit to give it, so there was no reason to discard it.
defence_argument: The acquittal should not have been disturbed since two views were possible; the husband was with PW-4 on the night, showing he was falsely implicated; a victim with 100% burns could not give a statement, so the doctor's certificate should not be believed.
legal_principle_applied: Appeal against acquittal: the appellate court may reappreciate evidence but must find the acquittal perverse or against settled law before interfering. Dying declaration: admissible and reliable if the declarant was in a fit state of mind and it was voluntary; a declaration made to a competent Magistrate with no animus stands on a higher footing; burn percentage alone is not determinative.
precedent_relied_upon: Sanwat Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1961 SCR (3) 120); Govindaraju @ Govinda v. State by Sriramapuram PS (2012) 4 SCC 722; Jai Karan v. State of N.C.T. Delhi (1999) 8 SCC 161; Rambai v. State of Chhattisgarh (2002) 8 SCC 83; Kushal Rao v. State of Bombay (1958 SCR 552); Vikas v. State of Maharashtra (2008) 2 SCC 516; Krishna Mochi v. State of Bihar (2002) 6 SCC 81; Zahira Habibullah v. State of Gujarat (2006) 3 SCC 374; Sakshi v. Union of India (2004) 5 SCC 518; State v. Sanjeev Nanda (2012) 8 SCC 450
